articles.title: Vietnam's supporting industries are penetrating deeper into the global supply chain. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam's supporting industries are penetrating deeper into the global supply chain.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
By investing in specialization and mastering manufacturing technology, Vietnamese businesses are seeking to enhance their production capacity and participate more deeply in global supply chains.
Two approaches to increasing domestic production capacity.
After 17 years of operation in the field of cutting tools, precision machining, and supporting industries, on October 15th, An Mi Tools Co., Ltd. (ANMI TOOLS) inaugurated its factory in Bac Ninh, targeting customers in the electronics industry. Currently, about 70% of the company's customers are foreign-invested enterprises (FDI). Since 2015, ANMI TOOLS has participated in the Samsung supply chain as a Tier 1 supplier.
The company has chosen to specialize its production facilities by industry group. The factory in Hung Yen serves the automotive, motorcycle, aerospace, and defense sectors; while the new facility in Bac Ninh focuses on the 3C industry, linked to the electrical and electronics sectors. According to Ms. Nguyen Nguyet Anh, General Director of ANMI TOOLS, the investment in the new factory aims to concentrate resources on industry groups with high demands for precision, quality, and product stability. The company is developing technologies such as multi-axis CNC machining, alloy sintering, laser machining of ultra-hard materials, vacuum PVD coating, and precision grinding.
The factory in Bac Ninh gives ANMI TOOLS better access to electronics manufacturing centers in Bac Ninh and Thai Nguyen . However, to maintain and expand orders from large corporations, the company must ensure consistent quality, competitive pricing, timely delivery, and product innovation capabilities.
While ANMI TOOLS focuses on enhancing its supply capacity for the electronics industry, TOMECO Supporting Industries Joint Stock Company chooses to invest in manufacturing industrial equipment, machining large components, and producing parts for export.
On October 16th, TOMECO inaugurated Phase 1 of the TOMECO SI Industrial Support Factory in the South Hanoi Industrial Support Park (HANSSIP). The factory was invested in to expand the production capacity of large industrial fans, precision machining, and OEM components, while also adding large, heavy-duty machining processes that the company previously outsourced. According to Mr. Le Quy Kha, Chairman and CEO of TOMECO, as order sizes and product complexity increased, the existing facility gradually revealed limitations in machining capacity. The new factory helps the company be more proactive in terms of schedule and quality control, while also adding heavy-duty machining, heat treatment, and precision measurement processes.
In the export market, TOMECO SI is manufacturing OEM components for partners in the United States . Over 40 product codes have been approved under the PPAP process, with an average export volume of 6-8 containers per month to Chicago. The company is also seeking opportunities to expand cooperation with international partners.
Besides manufacturing, TOMECO participates in research and development of equipment manufacturing technology. A state-level science and technology project on the design and manufacture of high-efficiency, high-capacity industrial centrifugal fans, led by the company, has been applied to the production line of Vicem But Son Cement Joint Stock Company.
The research, design, simulation, manufacturing, and testing processes demonstrate that domestic enterprises have the capacity to participate more deeply in technical stages, rather than simply processing according to existing drawings. This also forms the basis for enhancing domestic equipment manufacturing capabilities, opening up the possibility of replacing some imported products when meeting requirements for quality, operational efficiency, and cost.
ANMI TOOLS and TOMECO operate in different segments but both demonstrate a shift in the supporting industries sector: investing in technology, raising technical standards, and becoming more proactive in production. One specializes in supplying the FDI ecosystem; the other expands its capacity in equipment manufacturing, precision machining, and OEM component production for export. These two approaches contribute to increasing domestic production capacity. However, to create a transformation on an industry-wide scale, the efforts of each enterprise need to be connected to the network of suppliers, technology, and markets, especially the FDI sector.

The challenge of collaboration to enhance the position of Vietnamese businesses.
In Hanoi, Phase 1 of the South Hanoi Supporting Industry Park (HANSSIP) has attracted domestic businesses such as TOMECO, Brother, and THT, along with several FDI enterprises operating in high-tech fields such as MITAC, Inventec, VSO, and TriO. The Vietnam-Japan Technopark complex was also formed through a collaboration between N&G Vietnam, the Hanoi Supporting Industry Business Association (HANSIBA), and a group of industrial enterprises from the Kobe region (Japan). Here, Onaga invests in the production of components and products serving the aerospace industry and participates in the supply chains of companies such as Boeing and Airbus.
Bringing together domestic and international businesses facilitates connections between production, technology, and markets. Speaking at the inauguration ceremony of the TOMECO SI factory, Mr. Truong Viet Dung, Vice Chairman of the Hanoi People's Committee, expressed his hope that the N&G Group would implement phase 2 of HANSSIP, gradually developing the industrial park into a model for supporting industries and high technology, contributing to the economic development of the southern area of the capital.
According to Mr. Truong Viet Dung, there are currently over 7,000 supporting industrial enterprises nationwide, but only about 1,000 have the capacity to directly supply assembly companies and multinational corporations; of these, domestic enterprises account for about 30%. The gap between the number of enterprises and their capacity to directly participate in the supply chain remains significant.
Having factories and machinery does not automatically mean the ability to become a supplier for large corporations. Businesses must simultaneously meet requirements regarding technology, durability, traceability, consistent quality, and delivery schedules. Therefore, according to Mr. Truong Viet Dung, the development of supporting industries should be evaluated based on design and manufacturing capabilities, the percentage of value added retained domestically, and the actual position of Vietnamese businesses in the supply chain, rather than just looking at the number of factories or the localization rate.
This requirement is directly linked to the direction set forth in Resolution No. 10-NQ/TW dated June 8, 2026, of the Politburo on the development of the foreign-invested economy in the new period. The Resolution emphasizes the need to attract FDI selectively, improve the quality of cooperation, and strengthen linkages between the FDI sector and domestic enterprises.
In the context of global supply chain restructuring, the effectiveness of attracting FDI lies not only in the scale of capital or the number of projects. More importantly, it is the ability of investors to transform their capital, technology, and market networks into production capacity in Vietnam, creating more opportunities for domestic businesses to participate in the supply chain.
This requires investment attraction activities to be linked to the development of domestic suppliers, the enhancement of technological capabilities, and the expansion of access to international production standards. When Vietnamese businesses can meet technical requirements, ensure stable deliveries, and participate more deeply in high value-added stages, FDI linkages will create a clear impact on domestic industrial capacity.
For ANMI TOOLS, experience participating in FDI supply chains shows that investment in machinery and human resources must go hand in hand with the ability to maintain quality, schedule, and stability of the supply. For TOMECO, adding processing steps at the factory helps the business be more proactive in production, but the effectiveness of the investment still depends on the ability to utilize equipment, maintain orders, and expand the market.
Besides their own efforts, businesses need support in accessing technology, standards, and customers. Samsung's smart factory development programs, implemented through the Ministry of Industry and Trade, were mentioned by ANMI TOOLS as an opportunity for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve their production capacity. The Hanoi Association of Supporting Industries Enterprises (HANSIBA) also participates in connecting businesses with management agencies, reflecting practical difficulties and supporting access to policies.
Mr. Nguyen Hoang, Chairman of HANSIBA, believes that Vietnam needs more domestic businesses to invest in technology, improve production capacity, and participate more deeply in the supply chain. The development of domestic businesses can create a ripple effect, attracting more Vietnamese investors and expanding cooperation with FDI enterprises.
Speaking with a reporter from the Industry and Trade Newspaper, Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Thuong Lang, an expert in international economics and trade and a senior lecturer at the Institute of International Trade and Economics (National Economics University), stated that expanding domestic production capacity is crucial in the context of Vietnam continuing to attract FDI.

articles.title: India is concerned about China's non-tariff barriers. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: India is concerned about China's non-tariff barriers.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman stated that China's non-tariff barriers are becoming the biggest obstacle to bilateral trade, causing India's trade deficit with the world's second-largest economy to continue to grow sharply, despite years of negotiation efforts.
 Speaking at an event organized by the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank (WB) in Bangkok, Thailand , Ms. Sitharaman argued that restrictions on access to the Chinese market are significantly hindering the ability of Indian businesses to expand exports, exacerbating the trade imbalance between the two countries.
 According to official figures, in the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year (April-September 2026), India's trade deficit with China reached $68.9 billion. India's exports to China during this period amounted to only $11.4 billion, while imports reached $80.3 billion.
 In the 2025-2026 fiscal year, India's trade deficit with China was projected to reach $112.1 billion, with Indian exports totaling only $19.5 billion and imports from China reaching $131.6 billion.
 Minister Sitharaman emphasized that India has repeatedly requested China to expand market access for products with significant export potential, particularly generic drugs, livestock meat, fruits and vegetables, and perishable foods. However, these efforts have not yielded significant results.
 According to Ms. Sitharaman, China continues to implement plant and animal quarantine measures and various other technical regulations, making it difficult for Indian goods.
 Nevertheless, New Delhi insists on prioritizing the resolution of disagreements through dialogue and negotiation, rather than resorting to retaliatory tariffs or establishing similar trade barriers.
 India aims to promote economic relations with China on a fair and balanced basis, creating a more favorable environment for businesses in both countries.
 Meanwhile, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning affirmed that Beijing does not advocate for the deliberate pursuit of a trade surplus, and expressed readiness to strengthen cooperation and harmoniously resolve each other's economic and trade concerns in order to promote the stable and sustainable development of bilateral relations.
 These trade disputes are unfolding against the backdrop of India seeking to reduce its trade deficit with China while still needing to secure supplies of essential raw materials and components, particularly strategic minerals crucial for high-tech industries. 
 New Delhi also hopes that Chinese businesses will increase technology transfer, contributing to improving domestic production capacity and strengthening supply chains.
 Indian officials emphasized that improving market access, narrowing trade imbalances, and strengthening technological cooperation will play a crucial role in boosting economic relations between the world's two most populous nations.

articles.title: India selling more to US despite tariffs, but China trade gap keeps rising - India Shipping News
articles.summary: India selling more to US despite tariffs, but China trade gap keeps rising  India Shipping News
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India‘s shipments to the United States are rising despite tariff-related disruptions. Simultaneously, exports to China are growing even faster, but the trade deficit with Beijing continues to widen.
So, if India is selling more goods to both countries, why is one relationship proving resilient while the other is adding to the country’s trade imbalance?
The latest figures offer a clue. India’s merchandise exports to the US reached $50.81 billion during April-September 2026, up from $45.73 billion a year earlier. This is an increase of about 11.1 per cent, according to the latest trade figures reported by the government.
China presents a different picture. India’s exports to the neighbouring country surged 40.7 per cent to $19.26 billion during January-September 2026. But imports from China rose 23.3 per cent to $125.19 billion. The result was a trade deficit of $105.93 billion, up 20.7 per cent from a year earlier.
India-US Trade: Exports Grow Despite Tariff Pressures
The rise in exports to the US is significant because Indian businesses have faced uncertainty over American trade policy. The first phase of an India-US trade deal is nearing completion, but negotiations have involved questions about tariff rates and whether Indian exporters will enjoy an advantage over competitors such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia.
According to a Reuters report, the proposed deal has reduced the announced tariff burden from the earlier 50 per cent level to 18 per cent, although finalisation remained pending. Now, the latest export numbers suggest that US demand for Indian goods has not disappeared despite tariffs. But they do not, by themselves, prove that tariffs have had little impact. Exports might have grown even faster without the additional costs, while some businesses could have absorbed lower margins to retain customers.
India’s overall merchandise exports rose 18.51 per cent to $259.89 billion during April-September 2026-27, compared with $219.30 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier. This was faster than the 11.1 per cent growth in exports to the US. In other words, US-bound shipments are increasing, but they are growing more slowly than India’s merchandise exports as a whole.
Electronics, petroleum products, chemicals and engineering goods have helped drive the wider export expansion. Electronics exports alone rose 70.44 per cent year on year to $5.31 billion in September, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
India-China Trade: Why The Deficit Keeps Growing
The China story is more complicated. India is exporting more to its neighbour, but it is importing far more. According to China’s General Administration of Customs, India’s exports to China reached $19.26 billion in January-September 2026. Imports from China, however, stood at $125.19 billion. The gap between the two was $105.93 billion.
The deficit is not new. India’s trade gap with China stood at $112.6 billion in 2025-26 as imports rose to $131.63 billion while exports reached $19.47 billion.
The key issue is the size of the two trade flows. Even when exports rise sharply in percentage terms, they may not be large enough to offset imports that are many times higher. China supplies India with electronics, machinery, chemicals and other industrial inputs. These products feed into Indian manufacturing, infrastructure and consumer markets. India, meanwhile, sells a smaller basket of goods to China, including ores, fuels, seafood and agricultural products.
This creates a structural challenge. Indian businesses can sell more to China and still see the trade deficit widen if imports remain much larger. For example, a 40.7 per cent increase in exports sounds substantial. But India’s exports to China were only $19.26 billion during the first nine months of 2026, against imports of $125.19 billion. The difference in the starting values matters as much as the growth rates.
US vs China: What The Latest India Trade Numbers Show
The figures below cover different periods because India’s official trade data follows the April-March financial year, while the latest China figures cited here cover the January-September calendar period.
What The Numbers Mean For India
Sohom Banerjee, senior economic and AI expert, told NDTV that the quality of export growth matters as much as the headline numbers. “The economic quality of this growth deserves equal scrutiny. Gross export receipts reveal little about the margins retained by Indian firms, the domestic value added within their products, or the employment supported by additional shipments.”
He also pointed out that higher exports do not automatically translate into proportionately higher profits or more jobs. Businesses may offer discounts to retain overseas buyers, while some of the additional costs associated with tariffs may be absorbed by exporters or passed on to importers and consumers. India’s electronics sector illustrates both the opportunity and the challenge. Rising shipments can lift export earnings, but the long-term gains will depend partly on how much of the product is manufactured domestically, rather than assembled using imported components.
Banerjee said India should use its export resilience to strengthen its negotiating position and productive capabilities. He also highlighted the importance of affordable export credit, timely tax refunds, reliable logistics and help with meeting international standards. The same logic applies to trade with China. Expanding exports is useful, but reducing the deficit will also require Indian businesses to become more competitive in products that China currently supplies in large quantities.

articles.title: Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement: Expanding export markets and attracting high-quality investment flows. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement: Expanding export markets and attracting high-quality investment flows.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
(Chinhphu.vn) - On October 18, according to plan, Vietnam will sign a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries after the parties successfully conclude negotiations in July 2026, ending a 14-year journey with 21 official rounds of negotiations.
EFTA is an intergovernmental organization established to promote free trade and economic integration, currently comprising four member countries: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway , and Switzerland. Vietnam and the EFTA bloc have held 21 official negotiating sessions. The most recent session took place in Iceland from June 17 to 22. On June 22, the Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade led the Vietnamese negotiating delegation to attend the EFTA Ministerial Conference in Liechtenstein to discuss the final outstanding issues to conclude the negotiations. On July 2, Vietnam and the member countries of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) officially issued a Joint Statement on the conclusion of negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between the two sides.
Over the years, trade between EFTA and Vietnam has grown steadily. By 2025, bilateral trade is projected to reach 4.8 billion EUR, with Vietnam recording a trade surplus of 2.5 billion EUR, demonstrating the increasingly important role of this cooperative relationship.
According to leaders of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Free Trade Agreement between EFTA and Vietnam will open up many practical opportunities for the Vietnamese business community. First of all, the Agreement contributes to diversifying export markets, creating conditions for Vietnamese goods to access more easily markets with high purchasing power and top quality requirements such as Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland .

Furthermore, the Agreement is expected to attract high-quality investment flows from EFTA countries into priority sectors in Vietnam such as high technology, processing industries, clean energy, green transformation, innovation, and human resource development. This is not only a source of capital, but also an opportunity to acquire advanced technology, management expertise, and sustainable development models.
For Vietnamese businesses, the Ministry of Industry and Trade leaders believe that cooperation with EFTA partners will contribute to enhancing competitiveness, gradually meeting higher international standards, and thereby participating more deeply in global value chains.
Conversely, with a market of over 100 million people, a strategic location in the Asia-Pacific region, and a network of 17 established FTAs, Vietnam also aspires to become a reliable partner and a bridge for EFTA businesses to expand their presence in ASEAN and other regional markets. This will create opportunities for long-term investment, production, and business cooperation, benefiting businesses on both sides.
Ms. Nguyen Thi Hoang Thuy, Vietnam's Commercial Counselor in Sweden, concurrently accredited to Denmark, Norway, Iceland, and Latvia, stated that the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement goes beyond a simple tariff reduction agreement. This message affirms Vietnam's continued commitment to deep and broad international economic integration, market diversification, partner diversification, and improving the quality of trade relations with developed economies.
According to Ms. Nguyen Thi Hoang Thuy, what businesses need to see is not only the opportunity to increase exports but also the opportunity to upgrade themselves. The EFTA market sets very high standards, but these standards are also in line with Vietnam's new development orientation of increasing added value, improving the quality of growth, and participating more deeply in sustainable supply chains.
Main contents of the Agreement

The Free Trade Agreement between EFTA and Vietnam is a comprehensive and highly committed free trade agreement covering many areas such as trade in goods and services, rules of origin, investment, intellectual property rights, competition, trade defense measures, government procurement, as well as trade and sustainable development. In addition, the Agreement includes provisions on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), cooperation, and capacity building to support the parties in effectively leveraging the opportunities arising from the Agreement.
According to the Agreement, for industrial and seafood products, EFTA countries commit to continuing the complete elimination of import tariffs on products originating from Vietnam as soon as the Agreement comes into effect. On the Vietnamese side, most import tariffs on industrial and seafood products from EFTA will be reduced and eliminated within a maximum period of 11 years.
For agricultural products, the parties apply a market opening schedule that aligns with the trade interests and sensitivities of each country. Several key EFTA export products, such as cheese, coffee, chocolate, baby food, and nutritional supplements, will enjoy a 0% tariff rate upon entering the Vietnamese market over a maximum period of 16 years. Simultaneously, EFTA also grants Vietnam preferential treatment equivalent to that offered in recent FTAs signed by the bloc.
Regarding rules of origin, the Agreement provides a comprehensive system of rules of origin to ensure that goods enjoying preferential tariffs truly originate from participating parties. A notable point is the mechanism for cumulation of origin between EFTA member countries and Vietnam, and also allows for extended cumulation for non- agricultural materials originating from ASEAN or EU countries if they have preferential trade agreements with EFTA. The Agreement also clearly defines origin criteria for each product group, methods of origin certification, and regulations on processing and manufacturing.
In the Agreement, the parties committed to simplifying and modernizing customs procedures, enhancing transparency, adopting international standards, and fully implementing the commitments under the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement.
The Agreement reaffirms the rights and obligations of the parties under WTO agreements on anti-dumping, anti-subsidy, and safeguard measures. At the same time, the parties commit to enhancing transparency and consultation before applying safeguard measures, aiming to limit the use of anti-dumping measures between the parties. Furthermore, the Agreement establishes a bilateral safeguard mechanism to address cases where increased imports cause significant damage to domestic industries.
The agreement establishes a cooperation mechanism to minimize technical and plant quarantine barriers to trade. The parties commit to enhancing transparency, information exchange, establishing contact points, and promoting the development of technical regulations based on scientific principles and international standards.
The chapter on trade in services is built upon the foundation of the WTO's GATS Agreement but with a deeper scope of commitments. The agreement includes provisions on national treatment, transparency of administration, payments and remittances, and separate annexes on financial services, telecommunications, international shipping, and the movement of natural persons. Both sides commit to opening their markets to a level equivalent to or higher than existing WTO commitments in many service sectors.
Regarding investment, the Agreement stipulates the principle of national treatment for investors of the parties in many sectors other than services using an "active list" approach. Sectors such as agriculture, mining, and processing and manufacturing are open to investment with some exceptions related to land use rights or investment review. At the same time, the Agreement affirms the right of each country to enact policies to protect public health, the environment, and respond to climate change.
The agreement also includes comprehensive provisions on the protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights, including copyright, trademarks, patents, industrial designs, geographical indications, trade secrets, and border controls. The parties reaffirmed their commitment to the full implementation of the WTO TRIPS Agreement and encouraged participation in further international treaties relating to intellectual property.
The government procurement chapter aims to enhance transparency, promote the use of electronic bidding, and strengthen cooperation among stakeholders. The agreement also lays the groundwork for further negotiations on opening up the public procurement market and emphasizes the role of public procurement in sustainable development and supporting small and medium-sized enterprises.
In the Agreement, the parties agreed to build a healthy competitive environment by preventing anti-competitive practices such as monopolies or abuse of dominant market positions. The Agreement also established a mechanism for cooperation and consultation through a Joint Committee to address issues arising during implementation.

Regarding labor, the parties reaffirm their commitment to implementing the Conventions of the International Labor Organization (ILO), promoting gender equality, and combating discrimination. articles.title: Gravita India approves additional investment of Rs. 94.42 crores in Rashtriya Metal Industries - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Gravita India approves additional investment of Rs. 94.42 crores in Rashtriya Metal Industries  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
Gravita India Limited has announced its decision to make an additional investment of approximately Rs. 94.42 crores in Rashtriya Metal Industries Limited (RMIL), a material subsidiary of the company. The investment will take place through participation in the rights issue approved by RMIL's Board of Directors. This move was confirmed by a regulatory filing submitted to the National Stock Exchange of India.
Rashtriya Metal Industries Limited is primarily engaged in the manufacturing of copper and copper alloy products such as strips and coils. The company exports its products to several countries including the UAE, USA, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Kenya, and Indonesia. RMIL, incorporated in 1946, reported a turnover of Rs. 1041 crores for the financial year ending March 31, 2026.
The transaction will be conducted at arm's length, ensuring adherence to related party transaction protocols. Gravita India Limited's pre-rights issue shareholding in RMIL stands at 99.5880%, which will slightly increase to 99.5881% post the rights issue.
This strategic investment is aimed at supporting RMIL’s general corporate purposes. The acquisition will be completed within the timelines specified in the rights offer by the subsidiary company, with the entire consideration to be paid in cash. No governmental or regulatory approvals are required for this transaction.
Gravita India Limited, with its corporate office located in Jaipur, Rajasthan, has positioned itself prominently in the metallurgical industry, and this continued investment in RMIL is seen as an affirmation of its commitment to expanding its subsidiary's capabilities and market reach.
The strategic investment underscores Gravita India's intent to consolidate its holdings in RMIL and strengthen its subsidiary’s position in the copper manufacturing sector.

articles.title: Chinese toy and gift makers look to tariff cuts to boost US orders - The Star
articles.summary: Chinese toy and gift makers look to tariff cuts to boost US orders  The Star
articles.full_text:
GUANGZHOU: Chinese toy and gift manufacturers are looking to benefit from reciprocal tariff cuts between China and the United States, with exporters reporting stronger demand from US customers and exploring new markets and product innovations to navigate trade uncertainty.
Christmas is still more than two months away, but Gong Yongqiang is already preparing for next year. Shuttling between the shop, factory, and warehouse, the Yiwu merchant checks raw material stocks and develops new festive decorations.
His shop in the “world’s supermarket” Yiwu, in eastern China’s Zhejiang Province, is lined with Santa Claus figurines in various styles and sizes, the kind that will sit on mantels across the United States by December.
A recent China-US tariff agreement has given him fresh reason to look ahead with confidence.
At their eighth round of economic and trade consultations from Sept 20 to 23, China and the United States agreed on product lists for US$30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions. The United States will reduce tariffs on Chinese imports, including toys, home appliances, baby products, kitchen and bathroom goods, and holiday gifts.
“I followed the consensus the moment it was announced,” Gong said. “It is undoubtedly a positive signal for foreign trade on both sides.”
Harley Seyedin, chairman and president of the American Chamber of Commerce in South China, said the consensus sends a strong signal to markets and investors, helping businesses gain confidence to invest, expand and create jobs on both sides of the Pacific.
“Certainty is the lifeblood of business,” Seyedin said.
Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, said the tariff reductions signal easing trade relations, although their effect on the overall US tariff burden on Chinese goods remains limited. Their significance, however, lies in creating room for lower tariffs on some non-sensitive products and signalling future policy direction.
Across China’s manufacturing and trading hubs, exporters are already reporting stronger demand from US customers.
At her 15-square-metre store in the Yiwu International Trade Market, Nie Ziqin has packed the walls with Halloween decorations ranging from glowing spiders and pumpkin lanterns to horror masks, offering almost everything an American household needs for Halloween.
“This is this year’s bestseller. One client ordered hundreds of thousands,” she said, holding up a light-up spider. Her factory is working overtime to fulfil cross-border e-commerce orders and ship goods to US warehouses.
“Many American clients are optimistic about China-US economic and trade cooperation,” Nie said. “Mutual benefit and win-win results are what everyone wants.”
Her orders are expected to keep growing, building on a trend that emerged even before the September talks. Her US export orders rose 20 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, with American buyers placing orders earlier than usual.
As the world’s largest Christmas goods hub, Yiwu supplies nearly 80 per cent of the global market and ships more than 20,000 varieties to 178 countries and regions each year. The United States remains an important market for the city. Yiwu’s exports to the United States reached 104.51 billion yuan (about US$15.55 billion) in 2025, surging 25.1 per cent from the previous year.
Further south, toy and gift manufacturers in Chenghai District, known as China’s “toy capital”, in Shantou, Guangdong Province, are seeing changes in both orders and price negotiations. Although Chenghai covers less than 400 square kilometres, it accounts for more than half of China’s plastic toy output and about one-third of global production.
“When tariffs go down, buyers’ costs fall, which leaves more room for both sides. Price negotiation has become less difficult,” said Guo Bo, general manager of Guangdong YiYu Craft & Hardware Electrical Factory Co Ltd, a supplier of plush Santa figures, snowmen and reindeer. Guo expects order volumes to increase by 10 to 20 per cent this year.
Qiu Zhihong, chairman of Shantou Dave Plastic Toys Co Ltd, also reported a recent improvement. His company manufactures licensed products for Disney and Universal Studios, with exports to the United States accounting for 30 to 40 per cent of its exports.
One US customer who previously ordered 100 containers is now ordering 120, Qiu said.
For businesses that weathered last year’s tariff hikes, a pickup in US demand is welcome, but it is only part of the story. From seeking customers in new markets to refreshing the appeal of traditional products, Chinese exporters are finding ways to navigate trade uncertainty.
In Yiwu, Gong has learnt not to rely too heavily on any single market. After the tariff increases, the US share of his sales fell from a peak of about a quarter to around 10 per cent. But orders from Brazil, Colombia and Chile helped fill the gap, expanding his customer base to more than 30 countries and regions.
He is also designing new products. This year, Gong has launched more than 100 new designs, adding sound and movement to traditional static Christmas figurines. He said such features typically boost profit margins by more than 10 per cent. He is now developing an AI-powered Christmas doll that can hold conversations, with a launch planned for next year.
In Chenghai, Qiu is taking a similar approach. Touch-sensitive AI toys are outselling basic models, he said, prompting his company to invest in smarter products and stronger brands. It is also working directly with retailers to cut out intermediaries.
For Chinese exporters, these efforts to diversify markets and innovate products are already opening doors.
Earlier this month, Yiwu merchant Tao Yang secured an order from an American customer for more than 2,000 embroidered denim jackets. The order was modest in value, but it showed how fresh designs and tailored products can help Chinese exporters win over overseas customers and build long-term business relationships.
“When the client came to Yiwu in September, we used AI-assisted design and fine-tuned every detail with him in person. That’s how we met his needs and closed the deal,” Tao said.
Tao noted that Yiwu’s robust supply and industrial chains, along with a keen understanding of the market, power this agility and enable rapid product design and scaled-up production.
Luo said Chinese exporters’ future resilience will depend on diversifying markets, upgrading technology, building stronger brands and expanding their international presence.

After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.
The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war, largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?
Here’s what you need to know:
What happened at Maashiq Palace?
The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.
Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.
The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.
What happened at the airport?
On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.
Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.
The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.
Why are attacks on Aden significant?
Aden is the interim capital of Yemen.
The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.
The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.
The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.
But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.
Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
The city has been hit before.
In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.
A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.
What reaction has there been?
On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.
He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.
Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.
Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.
“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.
The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.
What is happening in the wider conflict?
Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.
Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.
The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.
On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.
In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.
Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

articles.title: Semiconductors and Thailand’s Electronics Industry - Chiang Rai Times
articles.summary: Semiconductors and Thailand’s Electronics Industry  Chiang Rai Times
articles.full_text:
Last Updated on October 18, 2026 by Jeff Tomas
BANGKOK – Semiconductors power the computers, data centers, cars, and appliances people rely on every day. Thailand already has a sizable electronics manufacturing base, and its exports include billions of dollars in semiconductor products. However, expanding into more advanced parts of the chip supply chain remains a longer-term goal, not a completed shift.
So what does Thailand make today, and what would it take to build a deeper semiconductor industry? The answer depends on separating established production and export strengths from investment plans and future targets. Start with where Thailand fits in the electronics supply chain, then consider Thailand’s national semiconductor strategy.
Key Takeaways
- Thailand has a major electronics export base: 2024 semiconductor exports reached THB 436 billion (US$13.8 billion).
- In 2025, electronics exports rose 15.7%, while ICs, semiconductor devices, and hard drives also recorded production gains.
- Existing strengths include PCB manufacturing and assembly, ICs, semiconductor devices, and hard-disk-drive production, including Thailand’s expanding PCB industry.
- BOI reported more than THB 700 billion in proposed semiconductor and advanced-electronics investment applications, which are not the same as completed projects.
- The national semiconductor strategy sets 2050 targets for investment and skilled workers, while deeper design and wafer-fabrication capacity remains a goal.
Semiconductors and Thailand’s Electronics Industry: What the Sector Makes
Thailand’s electronics industry covers several steps in the semiconductor supply chain, but a large manufacturing base does not mean the country makes every chip it uses. To see where Thailand fits, it helps to separate chip production from the electronics products built around chips.
How chips move from design to finished electronics
Chipmakers first design a circuit, which sets out how a chip will process or control electrical signals. Next, a fabrication plant, or fab, builds the circuit onto a silicon wafer, a thin round slice of material. Each wafer holds many chips, which manufacturers cut apart after fabrication.
The separated chips then go through assembly and testing. Assembly places a chip in a protective package and connects it to other components. Testing checks that it works as intended and meets specifications. These steps matter because a chip must be reliable before a manufacturer installs it in a finished product.
After testing, chips become part of larger systems. A computer uses processors and memory chips to run programs, while storage systems combine electronics with hard disk drives or other storage devices. Cars rely on chips to control functions such as engine management and safety systems. In appliances, chips regulate features such as temperature and motor speed.
Where Thailand fits in the supply chain today
Thailand has an established electronics manufacturing base, including printed circuit boards (PCBs), semiconductor devices, integrated circuits (ICs), and hard disk drives. A PCB is a board that connects electronic components; when manufacturers attach components to it, the result is a printed circuit board assembly, or PCBA. These boards are found inside computers, cars, and appliances.
The Office of Industrial Economics reported higher production in 2025 for several electronics products, including ICs, semiconductor devices, PCBAs, and hard disk drives. That activity shows Thailand’s role in making components and assembling electronic products. It does not, by itself, show which chip designs or fabrication processes take place domestically, or how much of each product’s value comes from local production.
Thailand also has activity in chip packaging and testing, steps that prepare chips for use in electronics. However, its established manufacturing strengths should not be confused with a fully integrated chip industry that handles every stage, including advanced wafer fabrication and design, at broad scale. The Board of Investment’s semiconductor and advanced electronics strategy describes a wider ecosystem as a development goal. Thailand’s plan for a domestic semiconductor supply chain reflects that ambition, while current production remains strongest in electronics manufacturing, boards, and related components.
Thailand’s electronics exports show where its strengths lie
Export figures point to Thailand’s established strengths in electronics manufacturing, including chips, storage products, and circuit boards. They also show why export growth should be read alongside production data: the two measure different parts of the industry.
Strong demand for chips, storage, and circuit boards
The Thailand Board of Investment (BOI) reported that electronics exports reached THB 1.86 trillion in 2024, equivalent to US$58.9 billion. Semiconductor exports totaled THB 436 billion, or US$13.8 billion. These are export values, not measures of domestic production or the amount of investment completed. The BOI’s 2024 export figures show the scale of the sector’s contribution to trade.
Momentum continued in 2025. The Office of Industrial Economics (OIE) reported electronics exports of US$60.989 billion, up 15.7% from 2024. Growth included integrated circuits, semiconductor devices, and hard-disk drives. OIE also reported production gains that year for several electronics products, including ICs, semiconductor devices, hard-disk drives, and printed circuit board assemblies (PCBAs). Export growth and production growth are related indicators, but they are not interchangeable: exports track goods shipped abroad, while production indexes track manufacturing output.
Together, these figures show that Thailand’s current strengths extend beyond semiconductor exports alone. The country also makes and exports storage products and board assemblies used in computers, data centers, and other electronics.
Why hard drives and PCB manufacturing matter
Thailand has a longstanding role in hard-disk-drive (HDD) manufacturing. Hard drives remain an important storage technology for data centers and other high-capacity systems, so local HDD production connects the country’s electronics sector to demand for data storage. In 2024, Thailand approved Western Digital’s plan to invest THB 23.5 billion in expanding HDD and related-equipment operations in Ayutthaya and Prachinburi. The investment announcement describes a planned expansion, not proof that the additional capacity is already operating.
Circuit boards are another important part of the manufacturing base. A PCB provides the physical connections between electronic components; PCBA production adds components to the board so it can function in a finished device. Because computers, vehicles, and appliances rely on these assemblies, PCB and PCBA capacity supports a wide range of electronics supply chains. BOI data also point to strong investor interest in this area, including foreign investment in Thailand’s PCB industry.
These export and manufacturing strengths help explain Thailand’s position today: the country has substantial activity in electronics components, boards, and storage, while a deeper semiconductor ecosystem remains a separate development goal.
Thailand’s semiconductor strategy aims to move further upstream
Thailand’s policy direction builds on its existing electronics manufacturing base while seeking more activity in chip design and wafer fabrication. The shift will take time: announced strategies and investment applications describe plans and investor interest, not necessarily new factories or production already in place.
What the national strategy is designed to change
The National Semiconductor Board, chaired by the prime minister, coordinates government policy and sets direction for semiconductor and advanced-electronics development. In October 2026, a committee reviewed a draft National Semiconductor and Advanced Electronics Strategy with milestones for 2030, 2040, and 2050. The phased plan is intended to develop a more integrated industry, including higher-value activities such as design and wafer fabrication.
The draft sets long-term ambitions, not current results. By 2050, it targets more than THB 2.5 trillion in investment and over 230,000 skilled workers, alongside a domestic semiconductor ecosystem capable of supporting “Made-in-Thailand” chips. The draft strategy’s investment and workforce targets indicate the scale of the government’s plans, but they do not show that Thailand has already reached those goals.
Investment interest spans several parts of the industry
The Board of Investment (BOI) received 517 investment-promotion applications for semiconductor and advanced-electronics projects between January 2022 and June 2025. Applicants proposed more than THB 700 billion in investment across chip design, wafer fabrication, testing, PCB production, and electronics assembly.
That figure describes the value proposed in applications, not money already spent. An application is a request for investment promotion; an approved project has received BOI approval, but may not yet have been built or fully funded. Completed investment refers to capital actually spent on a project. Keeping these categories separate helps avoid treating a large pipeline as operating capacity.
The range of proposed activities also shows how policy seeks to connect Thailand’s current strengths in boards and electronics manufacturing with more advanced semiconductor work. However, the application total alone does not confirm which projects will proceed or when production will begin.
Incentives can help attract higher-value projects
BOI promotion combines tax incentives with support for infrastructure, technology and innovation, workforce skills, and global business links. Together, these measures are meant to make it easier for companies to establish or expand projects in Thailand, including activities further upstream in the chip supply cha

articles.title: Russian embassy highlights Egypt industrial zone, website details 2030 operating target - Urban & Transport - Egypt - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Russian embassy highlights Egypt industrial zone, website details 2030 operating target - Urban & Transport - Egypt  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Russia’s embassy in Cairo highlighted on Friday the establishment of a Russian Industrial Zone in Egypt’s Suez Canal Economic Zone. It directed investors to a website outlining manufacturing opportunities, incentives, and development plans.
The embassy described the project as a special commercial and industrial complex for Russian companies in Ain Sokhna and East Port Said. Its post follows the July announcement of a selected developer.
The linked website provides detailed plans for a 50-hectare site at Ain Sokhna, with design and construction scheduled for 2026–2029 and operations targeted for 2030. It does not provide a corresponding timetable or land area for East Port Said.
Available in Russian, English, Arabic, and Chinese, the website combines a project presentation with practical guidance for prospective manufacturers. Its navigation covers advantages, infrastructure, industries, resident arrangements, and project background, along with a 14-question investor guide and inquiry forms.
The information is accompanied by port and factory imagery, maps of export destinations and SCZone facilities, and graphics explaining incentives. Historical remarks by the Egyptian and Russian presidents frame the project as a platform for industrial cooperation and exports to Africa.
Development plans and investor support
The project’s background page traces its framework to the intergovernmental agreement signed in 2018. In May 2025, SCZone and the Russian project company settled commercial terms for long-term use of the Ain Sokhna site.
The website identifies the Crystal Fund as the integrated development institution implementing the project with Russia’s Ministry of Industry and Trade. An agreement with the ministry made the fund the single point of contact for investors, developers, and future residents.
The fund’s services cover market research, project development and buyer identification; construction and utility coordination; and subsequent licensing, customs, and logistics support. The website says these services carry a fixed charge and a success fee.
It identifies Alexander Galushka as fund president, Alexander Krutikov as managing partner, and Alexander Shatunov as senior partner and head of the Egyptian project.
Manufacturers could build their own facilities on serviced plots, potentially with concessional financing, or lease premises built to their specifications. Proposed infrastructure includes electricity, gas, water, sewerage, roads, railway access and warehousing.
Manufacturing and market access
The website targets machinery, metalworking, chemicals, construction materials, transport and energy equipment, agricultural machinery, pharmaceuticals, food processing and industrial components. The background page additionally identifies petrochemicals, radio electronics, electrical equipment and timber processing.
Egypt has also sought investment from Tatarstan firms as part of its efforts to attract Russian manufacturers.
The resident guide says products could reach Egypt and overseas markets through the country’s trade agreements, subject to origin requirements and certification. The homepage advertises potential preferential access to more than 70 countries with approximately two billion consumers, while distinguishing China, India, and North America as international shipping destinations.
Residents may sell their entire output domestically, subject to applicable Egyptian taxes and customs payments. The website’s local-content references vary between at least 30 percent and more than 30 percent; eligibility for preferential exports would depend on each trade agreement.
Incentives and applications
The resident guide describes zero customs duty on eligible construction and operating imports, zero VAT on manufacturing inputs within the zone, and a three-year rent grace period.
It also outlines a deduction from net taxable profit equal to 50 percent of investment costs, subject to legal limits and capped at seven years. Elsewhere, the website calls this a corporate tax refund, leaving the precise mechanism requiring confirmation under the applicable rules.
Additional arrangements listed include full foreign ownership and renewable five-year residence permits for foreign investors.
Applicants must prepare expected products and output, building and land requirements, utility demand, imported equipment and materials, target markets, desired local content, and a proposed launch date.
The process moves from an inquiry to assessment, an individual location proposal, agreement on operating terms, and implementation support. The initial assessment creates no investment obligation, and launch timing depends on each factory’s readiness and construction requirements.
The online form requests contact and company information, sector and project details, and consent to personal data processing. The project also lists the email address rpz-egypt@crystalfund.ru and telephone number +7 (495) 129-04-44.
The zone forms part of wider Egyptian-Russian economic cooperation. Separate discussions have examined a regional grain logistics hub involving Russian exporters.
Across SCZone, Egypt inaugurated nine industrial projects worth $84.5 million in September, with nearly 2,000 jobs expected.

articles.title: Germany's draft Investment Screening Act: Implications for cross-border transactions explained - Freshfields
articles.summary: Germany's draft Investment Screening Act: Implications for cross-border transactions explained  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
A key area of changes deals with the question of what level of influence on German companies is significant enough to become notifiable – including a readjustment of voting rights thresholds, and expansions of the catch-all concepts of “atypical influence” and circumvention. Another change affects all situations in which a company holds shares on account of someone else. These changes are intended to close alleged “gaps” in the Ministry’s screening net.
Tailored voting thresholds
Standard initial screening triggers remain at 10% (for defence and critical infrastructure) and 25% (for other sensitive sectors). Subsequent acquisitions will trigger reviews at 50%, 75%, and a new 100% threshold, which captures full buyouts from existing majority control. The intermediate 20% and 40% thresholds will be abolished. This removes unnecessary regulatory friction and simplifies incremental stake-building in private companies. For publicly traded companies, the draft introduces dedicated thresholds of 15% and 30%. The 30% threshold is inspired by German takeover law and the 15% threshold captures anchor stakes that often confer de facto influence due to low attendance at annual general meetings. Furthermore, the Ministry is empowered to establish, by statutory ordinance, differing or additional screening thresholds.
The draft also introduces a new 100% threshold. This is unprecedented; under current law, the highest statutory threshold is 75%. This provision would be applicable to all companies, not just listed companies. From a corporate governance and security perspective, this new threshold appears to make little sense. Once an investor holds 75% of the voting rights, any blocking minority under German corporate law is already eliminated. The shareholder already exercises complete strategic control. For listed companies with an initial 15% threshold, an 85% threshold would mirror the loss of a 15% blocking stake. Pushing the threshold all the way to 100%, however, appears to lack substantive justification. Instead, it creates an unnecessary regulatory hurdle for routine corporate clean-ups, minority buyouts, and statutory squeeze-outs where no additional control is gained.
Atypical influence decoupled from voting stakes
Atypical influence is a concept that allows the Ministry to treat board seats, veto rights, or information rights like voting shares if they grant comparable influence.
The draft sensibly renames ‘atypical control’ to ‘atypical influence’, appropriately reflecting that these cases by no means involve an acquisition of corporate control. The current test requires the acquisition of at least some voting rights alongside additional influence. The draft expands this so that securing board seats, strategic veto rights, or sensitive information access can trigger review even without acquiring any voting rights. In the view of the Ministry this closes a loophole which, according to the Ministry, was previously used to avoid review. But by triggering screening without any share purchase, the draft removes investment control from the M&A process. Instead of screening transactions, it effectively creates a permanent, ongoing review of routine corporate governance.
Asset deals and IP licensing
The Draft IPG clarifies the perimeter of covered asset transactions, confirming that the acquisition of essential business assets “in whole or in substantial part” or significant domestic real estate triggers review. 
Crucially for the tech sector, the draft refrains from introducing a general, standalone screening trigger for licence agreements. Commercial licences will not be caught. Licensing arrangements will only face screening if the licensed intellectual property constitutes the target’s essential operational assets or if the structure serves to circumvent the rules.
Expansive ‘object or effect’ anti-circumvention rule 
The anti-circumvention rule has long been a key priority for the Ministry, which has grown increasingly frustrated with deal structures designed to sit just below statutory thresholds for purported tax or commercial reasons. While the Ministry previously had to prove that parties acted with a deliberate intent to evade investment screening, the Draft IPG now introduces an objective “object and effect test”. Going forward, the Ministry will no longer need to demonstrate that the parties acted with the deliberate intent to avoid review; it will be sufficient that the transaction structure objectively results in evading review. 
Read literally, the new provision could have an extremely broad scope of application as many – completely legitimate transaction structures – could have as their “effect” that German investment screening law is not applicable. The draft offers little guidance on where the line will be drawn. Although the Ministry drew inspiration from European antitrust law, competition case law will be of limited help in practice, as the standard is applied here in an entirely different context. 
Transactions most likely to attract scrutiny under this rule include the divergence of capital and voting rights and synthetic control structures. Dealmakers can no longer take comfort simply from staying under the percentage triggers if the deal effectively bypasses screening in practice.
Holding voting rights “on account” of someone else
Under the draft IPG, the investment screening regime would also cover situations in which a person holds voting rights “on account” of someone else. According to the draft’s explanatory memorandum, voting rights are attributed to whoever bears the “economic risk” of the investment, presuming that economic exposure translates into actual voting influence. The memorandum explicitly confirms that this covers both trustee arrangements and fund structures. Phrased so broadly, this may trigger mandatory filings for passive financial capital, which should not be in the Ministry’s own interest. Beyond these expressly cited examples, the exact scope of this provision is not clear in practice It remains open how this rule will be applied to capital market instruments such as depositary receipts, total return swaps, or synthetic equity, where investors bear economic risk without holding governance or voting rights.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened."
"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said.
He added any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorization "if it is requested of us."
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defense."

On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi Arabia accused Tehran of encouraging the group's escalation.
In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option."
The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, which also includes armed groups in Iraq.
