articles.title: Euronews crew say they were encircled and robbed covering protests - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Euronews crew say they were encircled and robbed covering protests  Euronews.comFrance: violence against journalists during protests requires immediate sanctions and implementation of our post-mission recommendations  European Federation of Journalists
articles.full_text:
Euronews correspondents in Paris covering the protests reported being targeted by masked individuals on Saturday’s major nationwide demonstrations following calls on social media to target media outlets and professionals to prevent coverage.
Euronews’ crew was assaulted by looters and rioters in Paris near the Place de la Republique on Saturday as they were covering the ongoing joint major protests organised by the so-called ‘Yellow Vests’ and student-led groups.
The crew was headed to another location from Place de la Republique – where the protests were being staged.
Shortly into their journey, they were confronted by masked looters robbing the nearby Intermarché Express supermarket on 14 Place Jacques Bonsergent, which diverges from Place de la Republique, and filmed it.
“We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us,” said Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris.
“They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing a gas mask, protective eyewear and a helmet, he was not seriously harmed."
"He managed to get away with just some bruises on his face," she added.
Our correspondent also noted that the looters stole their camera during the scuffles, which was eventually brought back by a group of youngsters who saw what was happening. The returned camera however did not have the SD card, and all footage recorded was lost.
Nilsson-Julien reported seeing things on fire in the area in the immediate vicinity of the supermarket, and loud police sirens.
“It is to be honest anarchy in the streets. There are many young people who seem like they are ready for a fight and looting going on. So, the calm protests of earlier today, at least in this area, are completely over,” she said.
Another Euronews correspondent, Valerie Gauriat, covering the protests at the Place de la Republique also reported a violent incident with a masked individual earlier while conducting an interview with a protester.
She noted that a protester slapped the back of her head and mumbled profane words as they walked past, denouncing media presence at the demonstrations.
The incidents come after certain groups on social media called on protesters to target media outlets and personnel, to prevent “the spread of misinformation” about the protests and reported violence.

articles.title: China Attracts Global Talent as Robotics and AI Industries Boom - Aktualita.co
articles.summary: China Attracts Global Talent as Robotics and AI Industries Boom  Aktualita.co
articles.full_text:
Beijing, Aktualita.co — China is increasingly attracting the attention of foreign professionals seeking career opportunities in the technology sector. The development of the robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), and new energy industries has become a key reason why the country is being considered a prime destination for international experts.
This phenomenon emerges as several developed nations face economic slowdowns, rising costs of living, and layoffs in the technology sector.
Amidst this situation, Chinese companies are continuing to develop innovation-based industries that require a workforce with specialized skills.
A Xinhua report on Saturday (10/17/2026) revealed a growing interest among professionals from various countries to build careers in China, particularly in sectors related to future technologies.
From El Salvador to China's Robotics Industry
Federico Flamenco, a 33-year-old engineer from El Salvador, is one example of a foreign professional who has successfully built a career in China's technology industry.
Flamenco initially completed his undergraduate degree in his home country before pursuing a master's degree in electrical engineering in China.
He now works at JAKA Robotics, a robotics company based in Shanghai.
His work involves developing robotics solutions for international clients. His ability to speak Spanish, English, Mandarin, and Portuguese helps him communicate with the global market.
"Working in the field of robotics was something I could only dream of before," Flamenco told Xinhua.
In his current role, Flamenco has the opportunity to handle robotic arms while witnessing firsthand the progress in humanoid robot development.
This experience demonstrates how the growth of China's technology industry opens doors for foreign experts to be involved in product development and industrial application.
International Interest Reportedly Surging
The rise in interest from foreign professionals is also being felt by international recruitment firms.
Miriam Wickertsheim, General Manager of Direct HR, a recruitment firm that assists international companies in finding executives in China, stated that interest in job opportunities in the country has seen a significant increase.
According to her observations, interest in working in China in 2026 has more than doubled compared to two years prior.
Direct HR has received inquiries regarding job opportunities from candidates originating from Europe, Australia, Arab nations, the United States, and South America.
Wickertsheim believes this condition is influenced by two interrelated factors: economic pressure in home countries and industrial growth opportunities in China.
Economic slowdowns, inflation, and waves of layoffs at various technology companies are prompting some professionals to consider other labor markets.
On the other hand, the development of the biotechnology, pharmaceutical, industrial automation, and smart factory sectors is creating a demand for new skills.
However, the increase in interest noted by Direct HR reflects the experience of that specific recruitment firm, rather than official figures regarding the total number of foreign workers entering China.
China Ranks Among Top 10 Most Innovative Countries
The appeal of China's technology industry is also reflected in international innovation rankings.
Based on the Global Innovation Index 2026 published by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), China ranks 10th globally.
The ranking assesses various indicators related to a country's innovation capacity, including technology development, research, infrastructure, and innovation output.
This achievement provides a picture of China's position in the global technology development race.
Growth in the high-tech industrial sector is also taking place amidst China's efforts to maintain economic stability.
Data from China's National Bureau of Statistics shows that the country's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 4.7 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026.
Meanwhile, economic growth in the second quarter was recorded at 4.3 percent year-on-year, lower than the 5 percent growth in the first quarter.
These figures show that the expansion of the technology industry is occurring while China's economy continues to face challenges in maintaining growth momentum.
Visa Policies to Attract Tech Talent
In addition to developing industries, the Chinese government is also preparing policies to facilitate the entry of specific experts from abroad.
One of these is the K-category visa, which came into effect on October 1, 2025.
This visa is intended for young professionals in science and technology fields who meet the requirements set by the Chinese government.
Compared to standard visa categories, this policy offers conveniences regarding validity periods, entry frequency, and duration of stay for visa holders who meet the criteria.
However, this facility does not mean that all foreign workers can immediately work in China without meeting applicable immigration and labor regulations.
On October 9, 2026, the Chinese government also issued new guidelines to accelerate the development of innovation-based productive forces.
The guidelines include 19 measures that, among other things, emphasize the integration of technological innovation with industry and the strengthening of talent development mechanisms.
Chinese Companies Also Opening Job Opportunities Abroad
Opportunities for international professionals are not only available within China.
The expansion of Chinese technology companies into overseas markets is also increasing the need for workers who understand local business characteristics and consumer needs.
One such company is Hydrexia, a hydrogen energy technology firm that is developing business in the United States, Australia, and Southeast Asia.
Hydrexia's Chief Financial Officer, Cao Jun, explained that Chinese companies have the ability to connect research, manufacturing, and technology application in industrial activities.
Hydrexia currently employs approximately 250 people in various countries. About 10 percent of its workforce is in overseas business teams.
The company plans to strengthen its international team presence over the next two to three years.
Expansions like this open job opportunities that do not always require professionals to move and settle in China.
Great Opportunities, Competition Remains a Challenge
The increasing need for experts does not automatically make the Chinese job market easy for all foreign job seekers to enter.
Technical skills, industry experience, language proficiency, and an understanding of the local business environment remain important factors in the recruitment process.
For international companies, changes in regulations and work permit requirements are also aspects that need to be monitored.
Meanwhile, for professionals, the decision to pursue a career abroad is not only related to the availability of vacancies but also includes compensation, cost of living, career progression, and residency status certainty.
Therefore, the growing interest in China's technology industry needs to be viewed in conjunction with broader labor market conditions.
While it is not yet sufficient to conclude that there is a massive migration of global talent toward China, these developments show a shift in the competitive landscape for international professionals.
China now offers opportunities not only through large-scale manufacturing industries but also through the development of robotics, artificial intelligence, clean energy, and various new technologies that require highly skilled human resources.

articles.title: RMG exports to EU fall 11.7pc as Vietnam gains ground - The Financial Express
articles.summary: RMG exports to EU fall 11.7pc as Vietnam gains ground  The Financial Express
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh's apparel exports to the European Union (EU) fell sharply in the first eight months of 2026, underperforming the bloc's overall import market as Vietnam gained ground and China maintained its position as the largest supplier.
Bangladesh's apparel shipments to the EU declined 11.7 per cent year on year to €11.92 billion in January-August, according to Eurostat data released on October 16.
The decline was steeper than the 3.83 per cent contraction in the EU's total apparel imports, which fell to €60.28 billion during the period from €62.69 billion a year earlier, the data showed.
Bangladesh market report
Industry insiders attributed the slowdown in European demand to geopolitical uncertainty, the Middle East crisis and subdued consumer spending. They said Bangladesh was also losing ground because of logistical disadvantages, domestic constraints and its limited capacity to respond quickly to orders for manmade fibre (MMF)-based garments.
Vietnam, by contrast, increased its apparel exports to the EU to €2.99 billion in January-August from €2.87 billion a year earlier, marking a 4.46 per cent rise.
China, the bloc's largest apparel supplier, recorded a 2.38 per cent year-on-year decline in shipments to €19.25 billion in January-August 2026 from €19.71 billion a year earlier.
Market data analysis
Inamul Haq Khan, senior vice president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), said China and India had faced difficulties in the US market because of tariffs in recent months and were aggressively offering lower prices to expand their presence in Europe.
Mijanur Rahman, managing director of Fabrica Knit Composite Ltd, said that amid the Middle East crisis, overall demand in the EU declined as consumers cut spending and prioritised essential purchases.
Explaining Vietnam's performance, Fazlee Shamim Ehsan, executive president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), said the country had an advantage in MMF-based apparel, supported by its polyester industry and access to raw materials from China.
"MMF-based garment orders are placed for small quantities with fast delivery," he said, adding that Bangladesh could not take all such orders because it had to import raw materials from China.
Vietnam also enjoyed a logistics advantage of 15 to 20 days over Bangladesh, he noted.
Industry leaders said the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) was adding to the competitive pressure. Under the agreement, EU tariffs on Vietnamese exports are being progressively reduced, with full elimination scheduled for 2027.
Meanwhile, several other major suppliers also recorded declines in shipments to the EU during the first eight months of the year.
Turkey's apparel exports fell 11.0 per cent to €5.10 billion, while India's declined 10.8 per cent to €3.07 billion. Cambodia's shipments dropped 4.51 per cent to €2.81 billion.
Pakistan recorded a 9.63 per cent decline to €2.29 billion, while Indonesia's exports fell 11.0 per cent to €608.88 million, according to Eurostat.

articles.title: Egypt Eyes Trade Agreements with Vietnam, Indonesia, and S. Korea - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Egypt Eyes Trade Agreements with Vietnam, Indonesia, and S. Korea  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Egypt is exploring new trade agreements with Vietnam and Indonesia while seeking to expand economic cooperation with South Korea toward a comprehensive economic partnership, as the government steps up efforts to strengthen export competitiveness and open new markets for Egyptian businesses.
The plans were outlined by Amani El-Wesal, Head of the Foreign Trade Agreements Sector at Egypt’s Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade during a meeting hosted by the Alexandria Businessmen’s Association, chaired by Medhat El-Kady.
Discussions focused on maximizing the benefits of existing free trade agreements, addressing barriers facing exporters and identifying new opportunities for Egyptian products in international markets.
El-Wesal revealed that 95% of Egypt’s exports are directed to countries with which Egypt has trade agreements, highlighting the importance of the country’s existing network of trade arrangements in supporting foreign trade.
New Asian Markets in Focus
The proposed agreements with Vietnam and Indonesia, alongside efforts to deepen economic ties with South Korea, reflect Egypt’s interest in expanding commercial and investment links with Asian economies.
El-Wesal explained that negotiations and studies concerning potential trade agreements are preceded by specialized assessments conducted in coordination with relevant stakeholders. The findings are submitted to the competent authorities, including the Federation of Egyptian Industries and the Cabinet, to evaluate their economic viability and potential contribution to investment, production and export growth.
The proposed initiatives could create additional opportunities for Egyptian companies to explore export markets, industrial cooperation and investment partnerships. Their potential benefits, however, will depend on the terms of any future agreements and the ability of businesses to meet the requirements of their target markets.
Business Leaders Call for Greater Use of Existing Agreements
Medhat El-Kady stressed that signing trade agreements is only the first step toward improving Egypt’s international competitiveness. The greater challenge, he said, is enabling companies to translate the advantages offered by these agreements into actual export growth and more diversified market access.
He highlighted the need to improve business awareness of rules of origin, customs exemptions and technical requirements, while providing more accurate information on untapped export opportunities, particularly in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
A survey conducted by the association among its members ahead of the meeting identified several concerns, including the complexity of rules of origin, non-tariff barriers and compliance with environmental and technical standards in overseas markets.
El-Kady called for closer cooperation between the association and the ministry through practical initiatives targeting specific export sectors and markets, with the aim of helping companies convert commercial opportunities into actual contracts.
Trade Information and Customs Procedures Under Scrutiny
Participants also examined the role of trade facilitation and regulatory transparency in improving exporters’ access to foreign markets.
Eman Nasr, Head of the Central Administration for World Trade Organization Affairs, outlined the WTO’s role in promoting transparency, facilitating trade and resolving commercial disputes.
She also highlighted the Egyptian Trade Information Portal, which provides information on import, export and transit procedures, including required documents, licences, prior approvals, certificates and other regulatory requirements.
The portal also offers information on the relevant authorities and logistical procedures associated with transportation and shipping through Egyptian ports.
Access to clear and reliable trade information can help businesses better understand compliance requirements, reduce procedural uncertainty and prepare more effectively to enter new markets.
Rules of Origin Remain Critical to Export Growth
Gomaa Madani, Head of the Central Administration for Trade Agreements, reviewed the benefits available to Egyptian exporters under bilateral and regional trade agreements, citing the Egypt-Turkey Free Trade Agreement as an example of how tariff reductions and exemptions can support market access.
He emphasized that companies must comply with the rules of origin and submit the required documentation to qualify for preferential treatment under each agreement.
These requirements remain particularly important for businesses seeking to take advantage of reduced tariffs, as eligibility depends on meeting the specific conditions established under the relevant trade arrangement.
Participants also discussed customs procedures, non-tariff barriers, technical and environmental standards, and ways to improve access to African, European and other international markets.

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Calorimetric Gas Sensors market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global calorimetric gas sensors market enters the 2026-2035 forecast period as a mature but structurally evolving component of the industrial safety and environmental monitoring equipment landscape. These devices, which quantify gas concentration by measuring the heat released or absorbed during catalytic combustion or thermal conductivity changes, remain the workhorse technology for detecting combustible gases in hazardous areas. Demand is anchored in oil and gas, chemical processing, mining, and utilities, where regulatory mandates for explosive atmosphere monitoring sustain replacement and new-installation volumes.
At the same time, the technology's trajectory is being reshaped by three forces: the build-out of hydrogen infrastructure, which requires robust detection of a gas with wide flammability limits; the digitalization of industrial facilities, which raises demand for sensor modules that integrate into IoT networks; and tightening environmental rules that extend monitoring to fugitive emissions and indoor air quality. articles.title: Advertising Espionage and the Global Surveillance Industry: Discover-Tech - Candiru and the Weaponisation of Digital Advertising - https://debuglies.com
articles.summary: Advertising Espionage and the Global Surveillance Industry: Discover-Tech - Candiru and the Weaponisation of Digital Advertising  https://debuglies.com
articles.full_text:
An institutional OSINT investigation into zero-click spyware delivery, advertising intelligence, identity deanonymisation, commercial surveillance networks and the strategic vulnerability of the global digital advertising infrastructure.
Scope: This assessment examines the Discover-Tech investigation published on 15 October 2026, its documented operations between 2024 and 2026, comparable commercial surveillance actors internationally, the regulatory exposure of the United States, Israel, the European Union and the United Kingdom, and the strategic outlook through October 2031.
Executive Summary — Bottom Line Up Front
The Discover-Tech case provides substantial evidence that commercial digital advertising infrastructure can be repurposed into a surveillance-delivery system capable of identifying individuals, collecting intelligence about their devices and, in selected circumstances, delivering sophisticated spyware without requiring an advertisement click.
The principal technical investigation, published by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab on 15 October 2026, documents 3,770,286,576 advertising bids, 441,954,291 apparently successful bids, 120,768 websites and 75,373 applications within its March–June 2026 dataset. It also links Discover-Tech’s advertising infrastructure to Candiru spyware attacks against at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera during 2024–2025.
A separate investigation by Confiant provides technical evidence of malicious advertising code, device fingerprinting, concealed command-and-control communications and connections to commercial surveillance actors. Its findings reinforce the central technical assessment, although the two investigations were coordinated and should not be counted as wholly independent corroboration of every allegation.
The consequential discovery is not simply that advertisements were misused to deliver malware, an established cybersecurity problem, but that an intermediary could combine the targeting power of advertising exchanges with specialised offensive cyber capabilities, creating an operational bridge between mass commercial data collection and selective device compromise.
The international comparison identifies several distinct categories of potentially relevant companies: spyware manufacturers, advertising-intelligence providers, mobile-location data brokers, commercial hacking intermediaries and ordinary advertising infrastructure operators. These categories must remain separate because technological similarity does not establish common ownership, operational cooperation or unlawful conduct.
The principal national-security concern extends beyond individual privacy. The same advertising architecture that allows companies to target consumers can expose the location, device characteristics, browsing patterns and potentially identifiable behavioural signatures of military personnel, diplomats, government officials, researchers, journalists and critical-infrastructure employees.
Principal judgment: Discover-Tech should be assessed as a documented example of a broader structural vulnerability in the digital advertising economy, rather than as evidence that every surveillance company uses the same technique. The immediate institutional requirement is to treat advertising-data exposure and advertising-script execution as interconnected cybersecurity, counterintelligence, procurement and regulatory risks.
The Surveillance Economy Has Crossed a New Frontier: How Digital Advertising Became an Instrument of Espionage
The Discover-Tech investigation exposes a structural failure in the global digital economy: commercial advertising systems can provide intelligence operators with access to individuals, institutions and devices that traditional cybersecurity controls were never designed to protect.
The revelations published on 15 October 2026 concerning Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech have exposed a contradiction at the centre of the global digital economy. Infrastructure developed to distribute advertisements and monetise consumer behaviour was used to support intelligence collection and the delivery of sophisticated spyware. Investigations by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab and cybersecurity company Confiant established links between Discover-Tech’s advertising operations and Candiru, an Israeli surveillance vendor placed on the United States Entity List in November 2021. The implications extend beyond an individual company or an isolated cyberattack. Governments have regulated personal data, cybersecurity, commercial surveillance exports and digital advertising through separate instruments, while the underlying technology has allowed these activities to converge. The resulting vulnerability affects national security, industrial competitiveness, financial institutions and the credibility of international regulatory supervision.
The numbers reveal an intelligence infrastructure, not an advertising campaign
The scale of Discover-Tech’s operations is central to understanding the significance of the investigation, although the figures require careful interpretation. Citizen Lab analysed 3,770,286,576 advertising bids between March and June 2026, identifying 441,954,291 apparently successful bids, with activity distributed across 120,768 websites and 75,373 mobile applications. Mobile applications accounted for 76.7% of the recorded bids, compared with 23.3% for web browsers. Within the analysed MyDSP dataset, Yandex represented 67.4% of recorded exchange activity, Google Ad Manager 24.74% and Vungle 7.24%.
These figures describe the volume and distribution of advertising transactions, not the number of individuals successfully identified or devices compromised. Their significance lies in the economic structure they reveal: access to programmatic advertising permits an operator to encounter vast quantities of device-related information before selecting a much smaller population for targeted surveillance. An advertising bid can therefore possess intelligence value independently of whether the operator wins the auction or displays an advertisement.
The geographical distribution reinforces the need to distinguish commercial reach from confirmed targeting. Citizen Lab recorded 457,283,658 bids associated with Yemen, 139,427,322 with Pakistan and 97,595,716 with Montenegro. Population-adjusted observations placed Montenegro at 156.68 recorded bids per capita, compared with 13.99 for Yemen. These concentrations warrant investigation, but neither the absolute volumes nor the population ratios establish how many residents were identified, which governments were responsible or whether particular devices were infected.
The decisive evidence concerns Al Jazeera, where Citizen Lab linked Discover-Tech’s advertising infrastructure to Candiru spyware infections affecting at least 45 devices during 2024–2025. The broadcaster’s network records allowed investigators to associate advertising interactions with subsequent spyware-related communications. The case demonstrates the transition from potential advertising exposure to confirmed intrusive surveillance, without justifying the extrapolation of 45 infections to the billions of advertising transactions observed elsewhere.
The decisive vulnerability lies between commercial data collection and offensive cyber capability
Discover-Tech’s importance derives from its position between two previously distinguishable markets: commercial advertising intelligence and intrusive spyware. Advertising exchanges distribute information about available impressions, devices and digital environments, while specialised surveillance suppliers develop capabilities to obtain access to protected systems. Controlium, the platform examined by Citizen Lab, connected advertising delivery with selective targeting and downstream code responses, creating a mechanism through which ordinary advertising activity could become an entry point for offensive operations.
Confiant identified device-fingerprinting functions, remotely controlled code behaviour and techniques capable of varying advertising responses according to the characteristics of the receiving environment. An individual did not need to click an advertisement for the delivery pathway to begin, although the execution of advertising code alone did not guarantee an operating-system compromise. That distinction separates the structural vulnerability of advertising infrastructure from the additional technical requirements of a successful spyware infection.
The consequences are industrial as well as operational. A surveillance vendor possessing expensive exploitation capabilities can benefit from an intermediary already connected to extensive advertising inventory, while the intermediary can provide identification and delivery services without developing the complete offensive technology independently. The arrangement potentially reduces the need to expose specialised capabilities across large populations of devices, concentrating their use on selected targets.
This commercial complementarity explains why regulating spyware manufacturers alone cannot address the entire problem. The intelligence value may originate upstream, where ordinary advertising transactions distribute identifying information, before any prohibited exploit is delivered.
Corporate fragmentation makes surveillance harder to regulate than to commercialise
The wider surveillance industry demonstrates how technological capabilities can be distributed across companies performing different development, ownership, financial and distribution functions. The United States Treasury’s actions of 5 March and 16 September 2024 identified a multinational structure associated with the Intellexa commercial spyware consortium, including companies established in Greece, Ireland, Hungary, North Macedonia and the British Virgin Islands.
The official record identified Cytrox AD as a developer of Predator spyware, Intellexa Limited as a technology reseller

articles.title: Iran War Triggers Inflation, Central Bank Raises Interest Rates - VOI.ID

articles.full_text:
JAKARTA - The surge in energy prices due to the Iran war has prompted a number of major central banks to raise interest rates to curb inflation. However, this move carries other risks. Economic growth could weaken further, even some developed countries could potentially experience a recession by 2027.
According to Anadolu Agency, quoted on Saturday, October 17, the United States Central Bank (The Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB), and the Bank of Japan (BoJ) raised interest rates in September 2026. Meanwhile, the Bank of England (BoE) maintained its interest rate, despite the continued increase in inflationary pressures.
Huw Dixon, professor emeritus of economics at Cardiff University, warned that the energy crisis due to the Iran war had changed inflation forecasts and the direction of monetary policy since the beginning of the year.
He assessed that economic growth could potentially stall by 2027. A recession is also likely in a number of G7 member countries, a group of seven countries with advanced economies.
"Interest rates have to be raised to control inflation. However, we may see interest rates remain high, but below the inflation rate, to limit their impact on the real economy," said Dixon.
The rise in energy prices has left central banks facing a difficult choice. Interest rates need to be raised to hold down inflation, but the cost of borrowing is also hitting households and businesses.
Dixon estimates that central banks will not return to implementing interest rates close to zero as during the 2008 financial crisis, unless there is a conflict with Russia.
US Inflation Soars, The Fed Raises Interest Rates
In the United States, annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September, from 3.4 percent in August, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.6 percent. A 9.1 percent jump in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the increase.
Overall energy prices jumped 20.4 percent compared to a year earlier. Gasoline prices rose 34.2 percent, while heating oil soared 74.2 percent.
Core inflation, which does not include food and energy prices, also rose to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent. Price increases also occurred in housing costs, education, used vehicles, recreation, and air tickets.
The Fed then raised its benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage point to 3.75-4 percent on September 16. The decision was unanimous.
The US central bank judged that inflation was still high so that a rate hike was needed to help bring it back to the 2 percent target.
However, the Fed still sees the economy as quite strong, supported by domestic spending, productivity growth, and investment.
European Inflation Rises, Britain Begins to Feel the Pressure
In the eurozone, annual inflation is expected to rise to 3.8 percent in September, from 3.2 percent in August, according to Eurostat's initial estimate.
Energy inflation rose to 18.8 percent from 14.3 percent. Inflation in the services sector also increased to 3.2 percent from 3 percent.
The ECB raised its three main interest rates by 0.25 percentage points each on September 10. The deposit facility rate, which is the interest paid to banks for funds deposited at the ECB, rose to 2.5 percent.
The ECB warned that the Middle East conflict could keep inflation above target for a long time.
The central bank estimates that average inflation will reach 3 percent in 2026, then fall to 2.5 percent in 2027 and 2.1 percent in 2028.
However, the ECB still projects the eurozone economy to grow 0.9 percent in 2026 and 1.4 percent in 2027. These estimates differ from Dixon's warning about the possibility of a recession.
The ECB sees higher-than-expected inflation risks, while economic growth is potentially weakening. However, the central bank has not confirmed the direction of the next interest rate.
In the UK, the BoE kept its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent on September 17. Six committee members supported the decision, while the other three wanted a rise to 4 percent.
UK inflation was recorded at 3.1 percent in August. The BoE expects the figure to reach 3.75 percent in the fourth quarter and slightly exceed 4 percent by early 2027.
Dixon said before the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, UK inflation was originally expected to fall to 2 percent in April. Interest rates are also expected to fall to a range of 3-3.5 percent.
Now, he estimates inflation will reach 4 percent by the end of 2026 and potentially rise further in 2027 if the war continues.
"The Bank of England's interest rate will go up," he said.
Although the BoE survey showed that the interest rate forecast lasted for quite some time, the movement of the financial market led to a possible increase. The BoE reminded that market prices are also influenced by risk premiums, which are additional yields that investors ask for to face uncertainty.
The increase in borrowing costs is beginning to be felt by the British public. The interest rate on fixed-rate home loans for two years was recorded at around 0.95 percentage points higher than before the conflict.
Japan Raises Interest Rates Despite Inflation Below 2 Percent
Japan is taking similar steps even though its inflation is lower than that of the United States and Europe.
Japanese annual inflation was recorded at 1.9 percent in August. Meanwhile, inflation excluding fresh food prices reached 1.7 percent.
However, the BoJ still raised its short-term interest rate target to around 1.25 percent on September 18. The decision was supported by seven board members, while the other two opposed it.
The BoJ sees its medium- to long-term inflation forecasts continuing to rise. The central bank is also concerned that wage and raw material cost increases that companies pass on to selling prices will push inflation above its 2 percent target.
The high price of crude oil, the weakening of the yen, and the increasing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) related products also add to the price pressure.
The BoJ expects inflation excluding fresh food to exceed 2 percent in the second half of fiscal 2026. The next rate hike is still open, depending on economic and inflation developments.
Dixon warned prolonged uncertainty could undermine confidence in the central bank's ability to maintain price stability.
"Inflation expectations over the past few years have been relatively contained. However, the current uncertainty is so great that this condition could change if central banks again let inflation get out of control," he said.

China's new-type energy storage industry is accelerating into a market-driven phase in 2026, characterized by a larger domestic market and value-oriented overseas expansion, according to the Equipment Industry Development Center of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
The shift is marked by significant changes in China's market scale and structure. By the end of June 2026, China's cumulative installed new-type energy storage capacity had exceeded 153 million kilowatts, a 50-fold increase from the early phase of the 14th Five-Year Plan (2020-2025). Independent energy storage has dominated the incremental market, with large-scale and long-duration projects accounting for a growing share.
"China's new-type energy storage installed capacity and application scale continue to expand, and both the market structure and global supply landscape are accelerating to optimize. Relying on China's complete industrial chain, cost advantages, and technological iteration capabilities, the global supply landscape is increasingly concentrating toward Chinese enterprises," said Wang Jianbin, a senior engineer at the center.
New-type energy storage has also evolved from a supporting role tied to renewable energy projects into an independent electricity market entity capable of participating in energy trading on its own. Tailored to local conditions, multiple provinces have introduced detailed regulations for market-oriented operations of new-type energy storage entities since the start of this year, providing institutional support.
Competition in the industry is also shifting from price wars to value competition. Overseas expansion in China's new-type energy storage industry is shifting from simple product exports to deeper localized operations, including overseas manufacturing, compliant business practices, and green supply chain development.

articles.title: Retail price impacts from the Iran war are uneven but add up for US households before midterms - AP News
articles.summary: Retail price impacts from the Iran war are uneven but add up for US households before midterms  AP NewsSee more headlines & perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
NEW YORK (AP) — More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and adding to the cost of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach.
Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the fighting disrupts Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores.
Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September jump in wholesale prices suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated.
The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said.
Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead:
Filling up fuel tanks is noticeably more expensive
BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or 45% above its prewar level, and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said.
Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to overall inflation by raising the cost of moving goods.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous and constrained, prolonging uncertainty over oil supplies and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild.
Higher airfares are hard to escape too
BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have raised ticket prices and fees, trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down.
Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates.
Any growth in grocery prices pains Americans after multiple years of food inflation
BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices can be volatile, and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs.
Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%.
Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after multiple years of food inflation. Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers.
A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries.
Rubber meets the road when it comes to shoe prices
BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027.
“Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said.
Transportation costs add up throughout product supply chains
BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices.
Consumers have felt the higher costs most directly when sending packages. The U.S. Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select, citing increased transportation costs. UPS, FedEx and DHL also impose fuel surcharges on many shipments.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping costs could remain elevated during the holiday season even if oil prices ease. Third-party provider AFS Logistics and financial services company TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter and the highest truckload rates since early 2022.
“We expect fuel to drive elevated transportation costs for the foreseeable future,” AFS Logistics CEO Andy Dyer said.
Although UPS and FedEx surcharges could decline if diesel and jet fuel prices fall, changes to carrier surcharge formulas, holiday fees and tight trucking capacity could keep total shipping bills elevated, AFS said.

These endorsements recognize the collective strength of Guzhen's lighting industry and mark the fair's rise from an industry exhibition to a national showcase.

All seven halls at the main venue have been upgraded, creating a new exhibition and trading layout in which each hall has a distinct theme and identity.
The seven-hall layout reveals three clear trends: increasingly sophisticated smart technologies, the return of design and aesthetics to the mainstream, and greater supply chain autonomy and control. Hall B, inter and commercial lighting, brings together decorative fixtures, residential lighting, and commercial lighting. Hall C, outdoor and special lighting, covers outdoor lighting, lighting for cultural and tourism attractions, and special-purpose fixtures. Halls D and E, lighting manufacturing and supply-chain, connect machinery, auxiliary materials and components, and supporting services. Hall F, smart home and living decor, combines smart home technologies with decorative furnishings and accessories. Hall H, new brands and cross-border sourcing, gives buyers a one-stop product sourcing destination.

This edition will assemble nine professional buyer delegations. Six domestic groups will cover smart lighting systems, decorative lighting, linear lighting, wholesale distribution, the full range of lighting products, and intelligent lighting. Under the banner "Hundreds of Businesses, Nationwide Connections: Leading Lighting Distributors' Sourcing Delegation," the fair will invite selected company executives and decision-makers to attend with concrete sourcing plans. Three further delegations will bring together key overseas buyers, media and associations, and key opinion leaders (KOLs).
This approach shifts the emphasis from visitor traffic to a sustained flow of orders. Using the IIRIS data management system, the fair will identify high-quality buyers, establish qualification criteria for major buyers, and build a year-round service framework. By extending short-term connections at the fair into year-round trade support, it will help exhibitors turn a four-day encounter into year-round business relationships.

The fair's flagship Hosted Buyer Program (HBP) will return with an expanded program, inviting hundreds of overseas buyers to join an international sourcing delegation. The business matching area in Hall H will host five Denggle.com Business Matching, four for overseas buyers and one for domestic buyers. The proven format combines pre-event research into buyers' needs, targeted invitations, and one-on-one matching in a dedicated meeting area during the fair. It will cover major lighting markets including Southeast Asia, South Asia, Europe, the Americas, and Africa.
A distinctive addition is the partnership with GZCD•STAR ALLIANCE for the "Stars Gather at Star Alliance: A Global Search for Lighting" event series. Activities will include a guided tour for 40 overseas buyers, store visits by KOLs, and the "206 Hosted Buyer Program Networking Party." Together, they will create an integrated program of exhibition matchmaking, direct sourcing at lighting malls, and social networking over cocktails.
This combination of exhibition halls and lighting malls, formal business meetings and informal networking, sets the Guzhen Lighting Fair apart. Behind the event is Guzhen's extensive local industry. In China's Lighting Capital, the entire town serves as a showroom, with opportunities to do business throughout the area. This is the foundation of the fair's distinctive strength: industry concentration drives efficiency, and location creates a competitive advantage that is hard to replicate.

This edition will feature five themed forums, all centered on light.
"Illuminating Prospects: Forum on Industry Trends and New Opportunities in Guzhen" will examine the reshaping of global trade and the direction of industrial policy, exploring how the industry can move from selling lighting products to providing lighting solutions and services.
The "Building Intelligence with Light, Achieving Low-Carbon Coexistence" forum will focus on green, low-carbon IoT applications, wireless AIoT lighting, and upgrades to smart manufacturing in factories.

They will cover industry trends, smart manufacturing, retail channels, health-focused lighting, and overseas expansion through new media. Their themes address both where businesses should go and how to get there. Combining strategic direction with practical methods is precisely the value industry dialogue should deliver.

articles.summary: Taiwan Is Planning $4 Billion Industrial Parks in Texas for Nvidia’s Suppliers  24/7 Wall St.See more headlines & perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Jensen Huang admits Nvidia can only fill about 70% of current demand, and Taiwan's government just backed a multibillion-dollar bet that moving suppliers to Texas soil changes that equation for both Nvidia and TSMC.
Supply is the tightest constraint on Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction). On its August 26, 2026 earnings call, CEO Jensen Huang said, “our entire supply chain is challenged,” and Taiwan now wants to move part of that chain to Texas.
In remarks reported October 16, 2026, Taiwan’s economics minister, Kung Ming-hsin, spoke. He said the government supports a plan for U.S. industrial parks, starting in Texas, with the first complex costing up to $4 billion. The parks target smaller suppliers that serve Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) and AI server assemblers such as Foxconn, placing them near Nvidia and other data center hardware makers.
The two names dropped on October 15, 2026, during a wider tech selloff over AI funding worries. Nvidia closed at $217.23, down 1.84%, and TSMC’s U.S. shares closed at $422.25, down 1.80%.
If you own either stock, the question is whether a supplier park matters to companies this large. It matters more to TSMC’s U.S. ecosystem than to Nvidia’s earnings.
What Taiwan Has Committed
The plan is a statement of intent, backed by government support. The Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association, an industry group, is expected to raise the money, and the government will offer loan guarantees, visas, and land access.
Kung Ming-hsin put each site’s estimated cost at $2 billion to $4 billion, and the government wants more than one U.S. location but has not set a number. Nvidia, TSMC and Foxconn have made no commitment to the parks, and no participating suppliers, schedule or customer contracts were named.
What Nvidia Gains From Local Suppliers
AI servers rely on smaller makers of power supplies, cooling systems, circuit boards, connectors and chassis. Placing them near U.S. assembly cuts shipping time and tariff exposure, which also helps Nvidia’s standing in Washington (we profiled seven of these non-chip AI infrastructure suppliers, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here).
One site is small, with $96.22 billion in quarterly revenue and $279 billion in supply commitments. U.S. production usually costs more, although forecast gross margin of about 74% suggests Nvidia has room to pass those costs to customers.
Taiwan also addressed AI hardware policy. Shipping restricted AI hardware to mainland China will become “a criminal offense under the Foreign Trade Act.” That lowers the risk of leakage, and Nvidia’s guidance already excludes Data Center compute revenue from China.

TSMC is also studying Texas. Describing capacity options outside Arizona on its October 15, 2026 call, management said, “And Texas is one,” and added that teams are evaluating options, with no investment announced.
Permitting, U.S. labor costs, and whether enough suppliers sign up are all unresolved. Larger Taiwanese firms are already moving on their own. Quanta Computer won approval to spend $973 million on server assembly in Tennessee, and Wistron won approval for $146 million to upgrade a Texas plant.

articles.title: 10 CEOs behind major companies that have exited Nigeria since 2022 - Nairametrics
articles.summary: 10 CEOs behind major companies that have exited Nigeria since 2022  Nairametrics
articles.full_text:
Nigeria’s business environment has witnessed a series of corporate exits, operational shutdowns and restructuring decisions over the past four years, affecting companies across manufacturing, technology, retail, energy and transportation.
From multinational corporations with decades of operations in Nigeria to homegrown startups that attracted millions of dollars in venture capital, several businesses have either shut down their local operations or scaled back their presence in Africa’s most populous country.
The departures have occurred against a backdrop of foreign exchange volatility, inflation, rising operating costs, funding constraints and changing corporate investment priorities.
However, the nature of these exits differs. While some businesses closed entirely, others sold their Nigerian assets, discontinued specific services or adopted distribution models that eliminated the need for direct local operations.
Behind these decisions are prominent global chief executives and Nigerian entrepreneurs who have shaped industries, attracted investment and overseen significant business transformations.
Here are 10 executives and founders associated with notable corporate exits and shutdowns in Nigeria between 2022 and 2026.
10. Shailesh G. Jejurikar — Procter & Gamble (2023)
Shailesh G. Jejurikar is an Indian-born business executive who became Chairman of the Board, President and Chief Executive Officer of Procter & Gamble (P&G) in January 2026, succeeding Jon R. Moeller, who led the American consumer goods company when it discontinued manufacturing operations in Nigeria in 2023.
Jejurikar has spent more than three decades at P&G, holding senior leadership positions across North America, Europe, Asia and Africa, with experience spanning the company’s healthcare, beauty, home care and fabric care businesses.
Before becoming CEO, he served as Chief Operating Officer, overseeing P&G’s Enterprise Markets, including Latin America, India, the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia and Eastern Europe.
He previously led P&G’s Fabric & Home Care division, the company’s largest business segment, which accounts for approximately one-third of its global sales and earnings. The division includes brands such as Ariel, Tide, Downy and Febreze.
Between 2016 and 2021, Jejurikar also served as executive sponsor for P&G’s global sustainability initiatives.
In December 2023, P&G announced plans to discontinue local manufacturing in Nigeria and transition to an import-focused business model amid challenging macroeconomic conditions.
The decision affected its $300 million manufacturing facility in Agbara, Ogun State, which had been commissioned in 2017 as part of the company’s investment in local production.
The restructuring came as foreign exchange volatility, rising production costs and difficulties accessing foreign currency placed pressure on multinational manufacturers operating in Nigeria.
9.Tayo Amusan — Shoprite (2026)
Tayo Amusan is a Nigerian businessman, property developer and founder of Persianas Group, the investment company that led the acquisition of Shoprite’s Nigerian operations in 2021.
Amusan founded Persianas in 1990 and built the company into a major player in Nigeria’s retail property sector, with investments spanning shopping malls, commercial real estate and retail businesses.
His company developed The Palms Shopping Mall in Lagos, one of Nigeria’s earliest modern shopping centres, alongside other commercial properties across the country.
In June 2021, Amusan led a consortium of investors through Ketron Investment Limited to acquire Retail Supermarkets Nigeria Limited (RSNL), the operator of Shoprite stores in Nigeria, from South Africa’s Shoprite Holdings.
The acquisition, whose financial terms were undisclosed, transferred ownership of approximately 25 outlets to Nigerian investors while allowing the business to continue operating under the Shoprite brand through a franchise agreement.
The transaction followed Shoprite Holdings’ decision to divest its Nigerian subsidiary amid foreign exchange difficulties, rising operating costs and a broader review of its African investments.
However, the Nigerian-owned business subsequently faced financial and operational challenges, including rising rental costs, inflation, supply disruptions and foreign exchange pressures.
In March 2026, several publications reported that Shoprite had completed the closure of its Nigerian outlets after more than two decades in the country, with some locations experiencing prolonged shutdowns and empty shelves.
The company, however, disputed reports of a nationwide exit. In an interview with Nairametrics on March 13, 2026, RSNL’s Chief Strategy Officer, Bunmi Adeleye, said Shoprite was undergoing restructuring rather than shutting down.
8.Luke Miels — CEO GSK (2023)
Luke Miels is an Australian pharmaceutical executive who became Chief Executive Officer of GSK on January 1, 2026, succeeding Emma Walmsley, who led the British pharmaceutical company when it discontinued direct operations in Nigeria in 2023.
Miels was appointed CEO-designate in September 2025, following nearly nine years at GSK, where he joined as Chief Commercial Officer in 2017, overseeing the company’s global commercial portfolio of medicines and vaccines.
Before joining GSK, he held several senior leadership positions at AstraZeneca, including Executive Vice President of its European business and Executive Vice President of Global Product and Portfolio Strategy, Global Medical Affairs and Corporate Affairs.
He previously served as Head of Asia at Roche, working from Shanghai and Singapore, after holding senior positions at Roche and Sanofi-Aventis across the United States, Europe and Asia.
Miels holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Biology from Flinders University in Adelaide and an MBA from Macquarie University in Sydney.
GSK announced its decision to discontinue direct commercial operations in Nigeria in August 2023, after more than five decades in the market, transitioning to a third-party distribution model for its medicines and vaccines.
The decision was announced under Walmsley’s leadership amid foreign exchange difficulties and rising operating costs.
GSK’s Nigerian subsidiary subsequently commenced the process of winding down its operations and returning capital to shareholders.
Miels now oversees the pharmaceutical group’s global operations, including its vaccines, specialty medicines and general medicines businesses.
7. Ladi Delano and Jide Odunsi — Moove (2026)
Ladi Delano and Jide Odunsi are British-born Nigerian entrepreneurs who founded Moove in Lagos in 2020 to address vehicle financing challenges among commercial drivers.
Delano previously established Grace Lake Partners, an investment and venture development firm, and served as CEO of JCDecaux Grace Lake, an outdoor advertising business operating in Nigeria.
He holds a master’s degree from the University of Oxford and a Master of Public Administration from the London School of Economics.
Odunsi previously worked at Goldman Sachs in London, where he held senior roles in the equities division, before joining McKinsey & Company as a management consultant in Lagos.
He holds a bachelor’s degree from the London School of Economics and an MBA from MIT Sloan School of Management.
Their company started with 76 vehicles in Lagos and subsequently expanded internationally. In August 2026, Moove raised $250 million in Series C funding at a valuation of $2.1 billion.
In October 2026, the company announced its Nigerian exit, with plans to transfer eligible vehicles worth approximately N35 billion to customers at no cost.
Moove disclosed that more than 9,000 customers had used its Nigerian services, generating approximately N57 billion in revenue through its vehicles.
6.Dara Khosrowshahi — Uber (2026)
Dara Khosrowshahi is an Iranian-American business executive who has served as Chief Executive Officer of Uber Technologies since 2017, overseeing the company’s global ride-hailing and delivery operations.
Born in Iran, Khosrowshahi moved to the United States during his childhood and graduated from Brown University with a bachelor’s degree in engineering.
He began his career in finance at Allen & Company before joining IAC, where he became Chief Financial Officer of its travel division.
He subsequently served as CEO of Expedia from 2005 to 2017, overseeing the company’s international expansion and acquisitions.
At Uber, Khosrowshahi has led the company’s transition toward profitability and expansion across transportation and delivery services.
In September 2026, Uber announced the shutdown of its operations in Nigeria and Uganda following a review of its business performance.
The Nigerian exit ended approximately 12 years of operations in a market where Uber launched in 2014 and helped introduce app-based ride-hailing services.
The company said the decision would not affect its operations in other African markets.
5. Sean Summers — Pick n Pay (2024)
Sean Summers is a South African retail executive who returned as Chief Executive Officer of Pick n Pay in 2023, having previously led the supermarket group between 1999 and 2007.
His career at Pick n Pay dates back several decades, during which he held senior management positions covering retail operations, corporate strategy and business expansion.
Summers returned to lead the company during a period of financial pressure, with the retailer implementing a turnaround strategy to improve profitability and strengthen its core South African business.
The retailer had entered Nigeria through a partnership established in 2016, opening its first store in 2021 and eventually operating two outlets.
The decision formed part of a broader restructuring programme under Summers, as the company sought to redirect capital toward its domestic operations.

HÀ NỘI — Japanese investment is helping drive green manufacturing and higher-value production in Việt Nam, as the country seeks to attract foreign capital that brings advanced technology, innovation and technology transfer, in line with a new policy direction under Resolution No 10-NQ/TW.
Japan has more than 5,800 active investment projects in Việt Nam, with total registered capital exceeding US$81 billion, according to the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade.
Free trade agreements (FTAs) between the two countries and their regional partners have also improved market access through tariff reductions, rules of origin and trade facilitation, creating opportunities for businesses to deepen their participation in regional supply chains.
Major Japanese investors, including Honda, Panasonic, Kao and Sumitomo, have established and expanded manufacturing operations in the country, while new investment projects in industrial parks are supporting the shift towards more sustainable production.
One recent example is Japan's Oji Group, which has begun construction of a $110 million aseptic paper carton packaging factory under its Oji Liquid Pak (OLP) brand at Long Thành High-Tech Park in Đồng Nai Province.
Nguyễn Quốc An, deputy head of the Đồng Nai Industrial Parks and Economic Zones Management Board, said large-scale projects of this kind could strengthen local industrial capacity and increase Việt Nam's participation in regional supply chains.
The management board would continue to support the investor during project implementation, coordinate with relevant agencies and address emerging obstacles within its authority to help ensure the facility becomes operational in line with regulations, he said.
Kestutis Sliuzas, general director of Oji Liquid Pak, said manufacturers, including packaging producers, increasingly needed to combine operational efficiency, food safety and production flexibility with circular-economy principles.
The company's project combines packaging manufacturing for the food industry with research and development, technical services, and the installation and maintenance of Japanese machinery, he said.
Japanese investment in Việt Nam also extends beyond manufacturing to research and development in the natural sciences, machinery and equipment maintenance, and the import, export and distribution of goods in accordance with Vietnamese law, according to experts.
Tsuchibashi Akito, chairman of the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Việt Nam, said Japanese companies continued to value Việt Nam's stability and development potential and intended to maintain long-term investment.
"We want to accompany Việt Nam in its industrial modernisation goals and achieve joint development through co-creation between Việt Nam and Japan," he said at a meeting in Huế on September.
Trần Việt Hà, deputy head of the Ho Chi Minh City Exporting Processing and Industrial Zones Authority, said the authority is seeking to accelerate project implementation by streamlining procedures related to planning and construction in order to facilitate foreign investors including those from Japan.
The authority also plans to move from handling administrative procedures on a case-by-case basis towards monitoring projects continuously, from investment preparation through to operation, Hà said.
Resolution No 10-NQ/TW, issued by the Politburo on June 8, 2026, on the development of the foreign-invested economy, sets out a policy shift towards attracting higher-quality foreign investment, particularly projects involving advanced technology, innovation, workforce development and technology transfer.
The policy direction reflects Việt Nam's ambition to move beyond labour-intensive assembly towards higher-value, technology-driven production, strengthening the role of foreign-invested enterprises in industrial upgrading and sustainable economic development. — VNS

articles.title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
articles.summary: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation RegulationUS corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influe...
articles.full_text:
US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.
Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found.
US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.
The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.
In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.
Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.
It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.
The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill.
Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.
Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.
Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR.
The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.
Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.
“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”
Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”
US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.
The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”
The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.

We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”
